turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through. We'll do the checks before you see the doctor. Pop the sleeve up for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Can we get this over with, I'm wrecked.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 146 over 92. Pulse is 76. Oxygen is 98 percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): 146? I get wound up the minute I sit in here.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does, in fairness. The parking was a nightmare as well, we circled the place twice.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I told you to leave it on the street.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): The repeat script on the screen says amlodipine 10 milligrams, once daily.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten? No. It's five. They brought it down.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He tells me five, but I've seen a box in the press with ten on it. I couldn't swear what he's actually taking.
[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): I'll not guess, so. Does he get it down him every morning?
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Not every morning. I find the tablet still sitting there some days.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it. Stop telling people I don't.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Grand. In you go, the doctor's just finishing a note.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, sorry. This screen's after freezing on me again. You're Declan Byrne, is it? Say it once more, it didn't save.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Declan Byrne. And I'm fine, so this needn't be a long visit.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's not fine. I'm Siobhan, his partner, I live with him. He's not sleeping, he's no energy, and he's lost all interest since the job went.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the cursor jumped. Say that again?
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Not sleeping, flat, no interest in anything. Since he lost the job.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm grand. She's turning a bad patch into a whole production.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Declan, the sleep. How is it, from you?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): It's rotten, if you have to know. Going on two months. Ah no, longer. Five months, easy.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Five months. What actually happens in the night?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I drop off, then I'm awake from half three, just lying there. Most nights.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And the next day he's useless. No energy for anything at all.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm tired, yeah. You don't have to narrate me.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I was back in the old notes. The low energy, since when? Say it again.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Since the job. Same stretch as the sleep.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the interest in things you used to like?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't seen a match since the spring. The garden's gone to weeds. I can't be bothered with any of it.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He lived in that garden. Now it's the chair.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): The job, I only half caught it. When did they let you go?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The warehouse, in March. No, February. Middle of February.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): February. And the mood itself, separate from being tired. Are you low?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm low. Flat, most of the day. I'm not dressing it up.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Snappy with it. I can't say a word right.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm irritable. I know well I am.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): How's the appetite?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat. I'm not off the food.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weight coming off you?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The weight's the same.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Apart from the blood pressure he's had for years, there's no other history. His brother has the diabetes though, and he's on metformin. That's the brother, not Declan.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Metformin, sorry, whose? Something dinged there and I lost the end of it.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His brother's. Declan has never taken metformin.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. Any chest pain, or trouble with the breathing?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the drink, since the job went?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of pints at the weekend. Well, actually, it's most nights now. There, I said it.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the true one.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I have to ask this gently, and I ask it of everyone. Any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn't worth going on with?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I'm not thinking of hurting myself, and I'm not thinking anyone's better off without me. I just want a proper night's sleep.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I've put that to him at home. There's none of that.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Can we move off it. I said no.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): You look tired, and a bit flat sitting there. I won't examine you past that.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any medicine, or to anything else?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): None. I've never had an allergy.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): What do you actually take at home, apart from this blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the amlodipine. She's always at me with her biotin capsules and I won't take them.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The biotin's mine, for my nails. He doesn't touch it.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Putting it together, this sounds like a depressive spell after the redundancy. I wouldn't lock it in today, but that's my working read.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Call it what you like.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll start you on sertraline, fifty milligrams at night, and I'll send you for bloods this week.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not starting a tablet today.
[SEG0063] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His brother was put on sertraline last year and he didn't sleep a wink on it. Declan doesn't need that on top.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, whose sertraline? Say it again.
[SEG0065] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The brother's. Declan has never been on an antidepressant.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): And I'm not going on one today. I'll talk to someone if I have to. No tablet.
[SEG0067] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. Scratch the sertraline, and leave the bloods. No new medicine today.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to the counselling service, and I'll see you back in a fortnight. If you're still this flat then, we can talk about a tablet.
[SEG0069] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing mild for the sleep while he waits?
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't add a sleeping tablet. Keep the bed for sleep, phone out of the room, same time up every morning, and ease off the pints on the weeknights.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Sure, if that's the best you can do.
[SEG0072] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry for sticking my head in. The amlodipine, five or ten? The list still says ten milligrams.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Five. I've already said it.
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't sort that off this screen. Don't change whatever you're on, and bring the box next time so we can read the strength.
[SEG0075] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Whatever's printed on it, he still skips mornings. I wouldn't say it's every day.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): I take the thing. Are we finished?

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Warehouse job and February redundancy supported; 'is not working' is not stated.
bad.text: occupation (description=Made redundant from a warehouse job in February and is not working, status=former, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Amlodipine current and nurse says once daily; actual current use disputed and dose unresolved.

omissions.text: Amlodipine dose is recorded incorrectly/incompletely: the repeat script/list said 10 mg once daily, but the patient repeatedly stated he is taking 5 mg; the true current dose remained unresolved and the recorded medication entry lists current use without this contradiction.
Patient stated he takes no other medicines at home apart from amlodipine; specifically he does not take the caregiver's biotin capsules.
Sleep pattern detail not captured: he can fall asleep initially but then wakes at about 3:30 AM and lies awake.
Low energy was also reported by the patient ('I'm tired') in addition to the caregiver's report.
History detail: the patient reported he has not watched a match since the spring and has let the garden go to weeds, illustrating loss of interest/anhedonia.
Alcohol intake detail is missing: he first said a couple of pints at the weekend, then corrected himself to drinking on most nights now.
The patient denied that anyone would be better off without him, in addition to denying self-harm thoughts and that life is not worth going on.
Family/medication history clarification: the caregiver and doctor clarified that metformin is taken by the patient's brother, and the patient has never taken metformin.

Planned sertraline 50 mg at night and planned blood tests this week were proposed, then explicitly declined/cancelled: patient refused antidepressant treatment, doctor withdrew sertraline and told him to leave the bloods, with no new medicine today.
Counselling preference/refusal detail: patient said he would talk to someone if he had to, but did not want a tablet today.
Doctor stated he would not perform any physical examination beyond observing that the patient looked tired and flat.
